subject: english-literature

moments.title: Shelley and Smith write competing sonnets
moments.who: Percy Bysshe Shelley and Horace Smith
moments.body: December 1817: Shelley and his friend Horace Smith have a sonnet-writing competition on the theme of ancient Egyptian power and time's destruction. Both publish in The Examiner — Shelley on 11 January 1818 (under 'Glirastes'), Smith on 1 February.
moments.takeaway: Shelley's poem is celebrated; Smith's almost forgotten. The pairing reveals how Romantic poets responded to news of antiquity (the discovery of Ramses II's bust at Thebes, then en route to British Museum, 1817-21).

moments.title: Ozymandias's afterlife
moments.body: Shelley's 14-line sonnet condenses a meditation on tyranny, decay and art's outlasting of power. Ramses II's throne name Usermaatra was Greekified as Ozymandias. The 'two vast and trunkless legs of stone' and the 'sneer of cold command' became some of the most famous images in English verse.

quote.text: Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!

moments.takeaway: Shelley died in 1822, age 29, drowned off the Italian coast. His political radicalism shaped much of his poetry.

moments.title: Continued resonance
moments.body: Ozymandias has been quoted in countless contexts — from Breaking Bad's penultimate season finale (2013) using the poem as a tagline to political commentary on fallen leaders. Its compression and image-density make it endlessly quotable.
moments.takeaway: GCSE study has made the poem one of the most-read short poems in English.

now.title: Tyranny and time
now.body: Ozymandias is a standard GCSE anthology poem. Its theme — temporal humility — speaks to every generation that encounters fallen empires. Modern readings emphasise Shelley's political radicalism — the sonnet is partly an attack on contemporary British royalty too.
now.open_questions: Who's speaking — the traveller, the sculptor, the inscription, the poet, the historian? The frames within frames are central to the sonnet's force.

reflection: Fourteen lines about a broken statue have shaped how English-speakers think about tyranny and time. Shelley's compression, his image of the legs without torso, and his sneer endure because the political pattern they describe endures.
